Price, Associated Press By — Didi Tang, Associated Press Didi Tang, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/chinas-xi-kicks-off-state-visit-to-washington-with-a-rare-planeside-welcome-from-trump Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter China's Xi kicks off state visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump World Updated on Sep 23, 2026 8:51 PM EDT — Published on Sep 23, 2026 11:16 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday, where he was met with a rare planeside greeting from President Donald Trump after their top officials agreed to extend a trade truce until January. READ MORE: Why Trump is rolling out the red carpet for Xi after years of slamming China Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the extension of the truce — under which the countries agreed to scale back tariffs and refrain from imposing new trade restrictions — during a Fox News Channel interview as Trump welcomed Xi at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington. "I don't know whether a bigger deal can be done. I don't know whether we will just roll the current deal," Bessent said in the interview, noting the extension to Jan. 10 could give the leaders more time to talk about the issues at upcoming international summits in China in November and Florida in December. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trade has been one of the biggest flashpoints between the two superpowers, along with artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan. But much of Xi's three-day visit is expected to be far more about pomp than substance, starting with Trump's decision to greet Xi as he landed, rather than waiting for him to drive up to the White House. READ MORE: As China and U.S. compete for AI dominance, both have shared concerns over safety A 100-foot (30 meter) long red carpet was unfurled at the bottom of the staircase placed at the door of Xi's plane. A 21-person honor guard was arrayed on the sides of the carpet and Trump and first lady Melania Trump stood near a staircase on the side of the plane, where they greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, with handshakes. The welcome ceremony also included a flyover by two B-1 bombers, platoons from each military service, and a presentation of the flags and anthems of both countries. Trump and his wife spoke to their counterparts, but their words could not be heard. Trump, who wore gloves and an overcoat though it was a relatively warm 63 degrees Fahrenheit (17 degrees Celsius) outside, removed one of his gloves to shake hands with Xi. At one point, he slapped Xi on the back and said something to him that was inaudible. "I think they appreciate it, tremendous people," Trump told reporters after he returned to the White House Wednesday evening. In a statement marking his arrival in the U.S., China's leader wrote that his country and the U.S. "should be partners, not rivals. Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand and the two countries can contribute to each other's success, thereby benefiting the wider world." Some Republicans have questioned the optics of the visit Beyond using the visit to try to keep "strategic stability" between the two countries, Trump has lavished praise on Xi as a "great leader" and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend. That is all while he has given Xi a pass on many issues. Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticized the "lavish welcome." Wicker, R-Miss., said during a speech Tuesday in the Senate that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader "based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. and China must interact at the highest levels because the countries are "the two largest economies in the world" and "probably the two most powerful militaries in the world." Danny Russel, a former U.S. diplomat under former President Barack Obama's administration, said the airport pomp delivered a propaganda win for Beijing. "Such extreme deference is valuable evidence that China's leader is now held in extraordinarily high esteem by the President of the United States. Beijing uses this at home and internationally to show China's — and Xi's — growing stature," said Russel, now at the Asia Society Policy Institute. China had hoped for a longer extension of the trade truce China had wanted a longer extension of the trade truce, which had been set to expire on Nov. 10. "It underscores that the United States is still concerned about China's full implementation of its commitments under the truce, particularly with respect to critical mineral exports and agricultural purchases," said Wendy Cutler, a former U.S. trade negotiator and now senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute. The tight timeframe gives the U.S. a chance to test whether China will deliver on unmet promises to buy U.S. farm goods, said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. "This is less about buying two months of calm than making China earn the next extension," he said. Trump has not yet commented on the extension. The two leaders are expected to talk about issues of substance more on Thursday, after an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Later, they will exchange toasts at a black-tie dinner, which will feature tech industry leaders like Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk. Trump to welcome Xi with 'the most respect' Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, telling reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new "work of art" helicopter landing pad would be ready for the visit while bemoaning that his massive White House ballroom would not. "I wish we had it for tomorrow night," Trump said again Wednesday. Trump on Wednesday was looking to match the pageantry he was met with in China earlier this year. Xi was not at the airport to meet Trump — Chinese Vice President Han Zheng was there instead. But a red carpet was rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing. A military honor guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, "Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!" also were present. The first lady said earlier Wednesday that her husband decided to personally greet Xi when he arrived in the Washington region because "they have a great relationship." "He's coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect," she said of Xi and his wife during an interview on Fox News Channel's "Fox & Friends." The long red carpet recalled a similar extra-long one the U.S. laid out for Russian President Vladimir Putin when he touched down at a U.S. Air Force base in Alaska last summer for a summit aimed at trying to find an end to Russia's war in Ukraine. On Friday, Xi and Peng will be back at the White House for a private tea with the Trumps before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries. Associated Press writers Mary Clare Jalonick, Will Weissert and Collin Binkley contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. WESTLAKE VILLAGE, Calif. (KABC) -- Former child actor Jonathan Taylor Thomas was arrested in Westlake Village on Monday, according to authorities.
The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said deputies spotted a vehicle stopped at the intersection of Westlake Boulevard and Townsgate Road, blocking traffic at a green light.
Deputies pulled alongside the vehicle to see if the driver needed assistance, and that's when they noticed that the driver appeared to be intoxicated.
While deputies performed field sobriety tests on the driver, the sheriff's department says the passenger of the vehicle -- identified as the "Home Improvement" star, whose legal name is Jonathan Taylor Thomas Weiss -- kept disrupting them.
Authorities said Weiss "appeared intoxicated, continually exited the vehicle and approached the deputies, distracting them from their investigation."
Deputies then attempted to detain Weiss for obstruction and public intoxication, at which point Weiss reportedly kicked a deputy in the stomach.
The former child star was then arrested and booked at the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff’s Station.
The driver was also arrested for driving under the influence of alcohol.
So far, no charges have been filed. The sheriff's department said the case will be submitted to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office for filing consideration.

articles.content_orig:
The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the nation’s most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong
WASHINGTON -- The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the nation's most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong, with a news outlet reporting Wednesday that China has obtained the F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office said in a statement that it and the Defense Department are aware of “a shipment issue" with F-35 components.
“We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles acknowledged that the jet components ended up in Hong Kong when responding to questions from reporters Tuesday. But he denied that the missing parts were “sensitive equipment.”
Australia is one of several nations whose militaries operate the stealth fighter jet.
“Yeah, so we are obviously working with the United States and obviously with its prime contractor Lockheed Martin, in respect of this,” Marles said.
He added: “My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Lockheed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday, when Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit with President Donald Trump. The Associated Press sent requests for comment to the Chinese embassy and Hong Kong's trade office in Washington.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that China has the F-35 parts — a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door — after the shipment was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while on the way from Australia to the United States for either repair or disposal months ago. It was not clear how the shipment was diverted.
Politico earlier reported that it prompted a congressional inquiry over concerns that China could have access to key components of the highly classified technology.
Beijing has kept tight control over Hong Kong since the territory was returned from British rule in 1997. Hong Kong cannot maintain its own military or conduct its own diplomacy.
The first F-35 Lightning strike fighter rolled off an assembly line in Texas about 20 years ago and was hailed as a technological leap. Since then, more than 1,200 of the stealth jets have been made and 19 countries have placed orders for the planes, according to the Congressional Research Service.
China already may have had at least some intelligence, albeit several years old, on the planes already. The Defense Science Board, which advises the Pentagon, released a report in 2013 alleging that Chinese cyberattacks accessed data from dozens of Pentagon programs, including the joint strike fighter.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” according to Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington-based think tank.
Bowman told the AP in November that American military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35's technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service .
Bowman said the plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat.

articles.title_zh: Eight US sailors in USS Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted suicide, Navy says
articles.content_orig:
Eight US sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide, Navy says
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during their lengthy deployment.
The disclosure was made in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York on Tuesday in response to questions from the Democrat on the well-being of sailors onboard following mounting concerns.
Family members of sailors had raised alarm about deteriorating mental health and grim conditions during a prolonged mission in the Middle East as part of the US war in Iran.
The carrier, which had been deployed since last November, is now returning to the US. The BBC has contacted the US Navy for comment.
In his letter, Cao said that there were five chaplains and multiple mental health professionals available on board to meet the "spiritual and emotional needs of the crew".
He said the eight sailors included "the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons".
While the US Navy has previously acknowledged supply challenges on the carrier, it denied that a mental health crisis was taking place on the Lincoln, which had some 5,000 crew aboard.
Cao's letter also denied widespread concerns about broken plumbing and shortages of fresh food, but acknowledged temporary "localized piping failures" and problems with the reverse osmosis desalination units, and some meal options were reduced for a "short time".
Senator Gillibrand, a member of the Senate's armed services committee, criticised the Trump administration's previous responses to reports of grim conditions, calling the treatment of service members "completely unacceptable".
"What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she said in a statement to the BBC on Wednesday.
"Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect," she added.
The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, was repeatedly extended.
In August, the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier, was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln following a nine-month deployment.
US sailors stopped in Thailand on their way home, hitting bars, malls and beach areas in their first time on land before continuing on to the US.
Suicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, while veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration.
A study of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" compared to other branches of the US military.
The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest".
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line or you can call the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline on 988.

Trump welcomes Xi to Washington as US, China agree to extend trade truce
Trump takes rare step of meeting foreign leader at the airport, underscoring the significance of US-China relationship.
China’s Xi visits US as Trump bets on stabilising global relations
United States President Donald Trump has welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to Washington, DC, for a three-day visit and high-stakes talks on trade, Taiwan and artificial intelligence.
Xi’s landed at Joint Base Andrews, outside the US capital, on Wednesday as the Trump administration announced that the two countries have agreed to extend an 11-month trade deal that offered temporary relief from punishing tariffs.
- list 1 of 3As Xi meets Trump, who’s winning their trade war?
- list 2 of 3What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
- list 3 of 3As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
Trump took the rare step of personally meeting Xi on his arrival, marking the first time in 11 years that a US president has greeted a foreign leader at the base, according to US media.
At the arrival ceremony, the leaders and their wives shook hands, spoke for a few minutes and stood for pictures as a military band played, cannons blasted and a B-1 military bomber flew overhead.
In a written statement afterwards, Xi said China and the US should be partners and not rivals, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. “He said that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world,” Xinhua reported.
Trump’s in-person greeting signals the significance that Washington ascribes to its relationship with Beijing, whose meteoric economic rise over the last several decades has transformed it into a global superpower capable of rivalling the US.
Xi’s visit comes after he hosted Trump in Beijing in May.
His schedule in Washington, DC, will include a state dinner attended by leaders of the US’s powerful tech industry, a military ceremony at the White House and a visit to the National Archives, home to documents of historical and cultural significance such as the US Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.
His talks with Trump are likely to cover the US-Israel war on Iran, the US-China trade deal, AI, and US ties to Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, according to analysts.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday that he had met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of Xi’s visit to “see if we could do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series of smaller things”.
“We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement,” Bessent said.
The agreement, which was set to expire on November 10, has now been extended to January 10, he said.
Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, said the short extension suggests the two nations were planning a wider deal.
“The two sides indeed have a bigger scope of negotiation coming to their trade deals, and they need more time to negotiate the technicalities,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that the truce was expected to hold even before the trip began.
Sun called Xi’s visit to the US “unprecedented”, saying “there has never been any precedent in the history of US-China relations for the top two leaders of the two countries to visit each other within a single year”. She described the stabilisation of ties as “quite prominent and very impressive”, noting that only 12 months ago, the two countries were escalating tariffs and export controls against each other.
On Taiwan, Sun said Beijing’s main goal would be to prevent or stall a $14bn arms package that Congress approved earlier this year, but the Trump administration has been unwilling to advance.
She said she expected the most progress on AI, where the two governments could agree on ways to manage their dialogue.
“We know that the US has proposed a hotline mechanism for notification to each other when there is a significant security risk associated with AI that happens in their individual country,” she said. “We’ll have to see whether the two leaders are able to make progress on this important issue.”

Ukraine sent two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea, Zelenskiy says
By Tom Balmforth and Brenda Goh
UNITED NATIONS/SEOUL, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Wednesday in an address to the United Nations General Assembly.
"Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea," said Zelenskiy in his speech.
"These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die."
Zelenskiy did not provide more details about the return. Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia's Kursk region in January last year. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be apprehended alive since the country joined the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
Zelenskiy said at the time that he would hand them over to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea, citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
South Korean opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told reporters on Thursday that the two North Koreans had left Ukraine last weekend, transited through a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days ago, Yonhap News Agency reported.
"While their exact location is unknown, I believe our intelligence agencies are protecting them," Yu was quoted as saying.
South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would not be able to confirm the matter, citing the need to protect the safety of the soldiers and their families. The country's Unification Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Korea in June said it would accept all North Korean prisoners of war who fought for Russia and opposed any repatriation of them to Russia or North Korea.
Zelenskiy also criticised North Korea for sending its troops to fight for Russia.
"This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? Kim Jong Un uses them like currency. And he gets something in return," he said.
North Korea has sent around 14,000 to 15,000 soldiers since 2024 to support Russia's war against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates. Most of them have been deployed in the Russian region of Kursk, where they helped Moscow's forces repel a Ukrainian incursion.
The country has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.
(Reporting by Brenda Goh and Joyce Lee in Seoul and Tom Balmforth in New York; Editing by Stephen Coates)

articles.title_orig: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.title_zh: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON – The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the nation's most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong, with a news outlet reporting Wednesday that China has obtained the F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office said in a statement that it and the Defense Department are aware of “a shipment issue" with F-35 components.
“We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles acknowledged that the jet components ended up in Hong Kong when responding to questions from reporters Tuesday. But he denied that the missing parts were “sensitive equipment.”
Australia is one of several nations whose militaries operate the stealth fighter jet.
“Yeah, so we are obviously working with the United States and obviously with its prime contractor Lockheed Martin, in respect of this,” Marles said.
He added: “My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Lockheed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday, when Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit with President Donald Trump. The Associated Press sent requests for comment to the Chinese embassy and Hong Kong's trade office in Washington.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that China has the F-35 parts — a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door — after the shipment was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while on the way from Australia to the United States for either repair or disposal months ago. It was not clear how the shipment was diverted.
Politico earlier reported that it prompted a congressional inquiry over concerns that China could have access to key components of the highly classified technology.
Beijing has kept tight control over Hong Kong since the territory was returned from British rule in 1997. Hong Kong cannot maintain its own military or conduct its own diplomacy.
The first F-35 Lightning strike fighter rolled off an assembly line in Texas about 20 years ago and was hailed as a technological leap. Since then, more than 1,200 of the stealth jets have been made and 19 countries have placed orders for the planes, according to the Congressional Research Service.
China already may have had at least some intelligence, albeit several years old, on the planes already. The Defense Science Board, which advises the Pentagon, released a report in 2013 alleging that Chinese cyberattacks accessed data from dozens of Pentagon programs, including the joint strike fighter.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” according to Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington-based think tank.
Bowman told the AP in November that American military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35's technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Bowman said the plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat.
Associated Press writer Didi Tang contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
Dolly Parton's sister Freida defends nephew after firing, restraining order
One of Dolly Parton's sisters is addressing the firing and restraining order against her nephew amid speculation of tension within the family.
She's Alive, LLC (SAL), the entity the late country musician designed to protect her legacy after her Aug. 25 death, filed a lawsuit Sept. 22 alleging her nephew, Bryan Seaver, threatened to smear his aunt’s legacy and made violent threats against several employees. The reported lawsuit and temporary restraining order came a day after Seaver received a termination notice from his role as his late aunt's head of security.
In a brief statement shared on Instagram Sept. 23, Parton's younger sister Freida dismissed the idea of a rift within the family and expressed support for Seaver, her nephew.
"Hi I'll say this and this only: there is no feud within our family. No one among the Parton/Owens family is fighting over Dolly's estate," she wrote. "We all love Bryan, just as we love each other. I love you all!!"
USA TODAY reached out to Seaver through his security company for comment.
Seaver, who oversaw the "Jolene" singer's security operations for more than 20 years, is the son of the late Larry Seaver, who previously held the position, and Dolly's younger sister Cassie Parton, 75.
In addition to working to protect his aunt, her residences and her professional properties, Seaver is the CEO of Squadron Augmented Protection Services, a Nashville-based company offering executive protection, estate security, business intelligence, K-9 services and event security, according to his LinkedIn page.
What is Bryan Seaver accused of?
In a lawsuit filed in Davidson County Chancery Court on Sept. 22, She's Alive LLC (SAL) alleges that Seaver waged a campaign of threats, harassment and intimidation on Parton's family and those entrusted to protect her brand.
Seaver is accused of threatening to ruin Dolly Parton's brand partnerships unless he was paid through podcast appearances and social media, according to the lawsuit obtained by the Nashville Tennesean, part of the USA TODAY Network.
The lawsuit also claimed Seaver made "threats of real-world violence" towards the singer's staff, partners, and legal and business advisers, allegedly often invoking his background as a military contractor during the Iraq War.
"As the entity entrusted by Ms. Parton to protect and promote her life’s work for future generations, SAL must cultivate a safe work environment for employees, advisors, and partners, free from intimidation or hostility — particularly intimidation by an armed former security contractor," the lawsuit reads. "Without relief, Defendants’ calculated campaign will continue to inflict fear, to destabilize SAL’s operations, and to cause further irreparable harm."
The lawsuit said Seaver allegedly told Danny Nozell, the country music legend's former manager who was selected by Parton to run She's Alive, "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or ... pay me."
What has Bryan Seaver said?
In a statement to TMZ shared Sept. 21, Seaver said he and his teams were "dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions" taken by Nozell and Pinnacle Bank.
"We remain unshakably resolved to fulfill her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much," the statement reads.
Seaver announced his aunt's death in an Aug. 25 video shared on social media, saying he first followed Dolly Parton on the road when he was a kid in the early 1980s and got a taste of the doors she opened for her family "to reach the potential we didn't even know was possible." In the video, he said that Dolly Parton personally asked him to reveal her death.
"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you," he said in the video. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not."
Contributing: Evan Mealins, Nashville Tennessean

articles.title_zh: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said.
Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

articles.content_orig: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. At the same time, a federal judge heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning the outlets from the White House. Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington this evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. And at the same time, a federal judge today heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning them from the White House. Our Liz Landers is at the White House covering both stories, and she joins us now. So, Liz, we will start with this state visit. What is the focus of it? Liz Landers: Yes, Geoff, President Trump is greeting leader Xi right now at Joint Base Andrews here in Washington for an arrival ceremony that has all the pomp and circumstance of this major state visit. This is the first time that Xi has been to the White House since 2015. And President Trump visited China back in May and was not awarded this same kind of pomp, circumstance and arrival. In particular, Xi did not greet him when he landed there in China back in May. You're seeing some of those images now. I will remind our viewers that those images are from several months ago because the White House TV pool is still not covering the president's events today. We believe that there are going to be a number of issues that will be addressed during this visit. A senior administration official told us earlier that AI, artificial intelligence, of course, will be on the top of the list, also some of these export controls that the United States has on our computing chips and selling those to China. The possibility of reducing tariffs on some goods is apparently going to come up, and also political prisoners. Several China watchers and experts that I have spoken with don't really think that this meeting is going to be so much about deliverables as it is about continuing to forge that personal relationship that President Trump has with leader Xi. I spoke earlier today with Kyle Chan. He's a fellow at the Brookings institute. And he was actually talking about these export controls, saying that matters less and less for the Chinese government because they are going all out to build their own AI chips themselves. And when it comes to artificial intelligence in particular, you heard some of that addressed from the U.N. today in Nick's story. China is not interested in a joint slowdown of AI development, according to Chan. He says that they're more worried about cyber risks, hacking companies, and they don't share, China does not share the same concerns that we have heard from U.S. AI companies and leaders recently that robots, AI may kill us all in the near future. Geoff, one more thing I want to add. Not everybody is happy about this visit and all of the accoutrements that are being laid out for President Xi. Republican Senator Wicker, he's the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, says that he would have advised against this lavish welcome to what he calls a brutal dictator. Geoff Bennett: And, Liz, there's a state dinner tomorrow evening. Who is expected to be in attendance? Liz Landers: Well, Geoff, as you would imagine, with all of this talk of AI and technology, there are leaders from several major business companies and AI companies that are going to be at the White House tomorrow. A senior administration official says that Jeff Bezos will be there, as well as Elon Musk, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, a chipmaker, and Sam Altman of OpenAI. The first lady, Melania Trump, said in a FOX News interview today that President Trump wanted to have the state dinner because they have a great relationship. She said that she's been involved in every detail of the planning for the state dinner tomorrow night. And she also -- and I'd also just add that this is only the second state dinner that President Trump has now had in his second term in office, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: All right, Liz, in the minute we have left, bring us up to speed on this lawsuit involving the three news organizations that were banned from the White House by President Trump. Liz Landers: There was a hearing on this, this afternoon, and the judge in this case, a district judge here in Washington, said right off the bat that he was skeptical of the argument that the Trump administration, that the Trump White House is making here on due process grounds. It sounds like the judge believes that the due process of these news organizations was violated. The government is arguing in a filing that they issued late last night that news organizations failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House. This has now turned into a conversation about national security. That is what the president and the administration are arguing is at stake here, that these news organizations somehow violated national security there. The judge also seemed skeptical of that, Geoff. We still do not have an answer from the judge as to whether the ban on Politico, CNN, and MS NOW will be lifted. Geoff Bennett: Liz Landers outside the West Wing at the White House for us tonight. Liz, thanks so much. Liz Landers: Of course.

articles.title_orig: Trump likely ‘smirked’ as 'crass' Iranian president lashed out at US in UN speech: expert
articles.title_zh: Trump likely ‘smirked’ as 'crass' Iranian president lashed out at US in UN speech: expert
articles.content_orig:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital Wednesday.
The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of one another, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount.
"Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us."
"I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record.
Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faces a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday.
While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
"To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said.
"Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now."
Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes.
Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive.
Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other."
But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework.
"It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said.
"In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic."
The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict.
TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN
"Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said.
Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy.
"I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program.
"Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved.

articles.title_zh: A Teacher and Activist Admits to Making Up Palestinian Background
articles.content_orig:
A Philadelphia teacher is facing criticism from her fellow colleagues and activists after it was revealed that she fabricated being both Palestinian and Black.
The Racial Justice Organizing Committee (RJOC) and Philly Educators for Palestine (PEFP) announced over the weekend that it was cutting ties with “one of their long-time members”, Hannah Gann, who “completely lied about her identity and background, claiming at various times to be Palestinian, Tunisian and Black”.
Members of both organizations met with Gann and questioned her about her background. After over an hour of discussion, Gann “finally admitted she lied”, the joint statement said, adding: “We asked her to publicly acknowledge that she is a white woman of Jewish heritage and an Israeli settler family.
“We will no longer work with Hannah, and she will no longer be welcome in any of our organizing spaces … We recognize the profound harm this has caused; Palestinians whose identity and struggle were appropriated, the Black community, young people, organizers, and organizations whose trust and resources were exploited,” PEFP and RJOC continued.
Gann released a separate statement on Instagram a few days later, saying in a video: “One of the most sickening aspects of facing what I’ve done is seeing the way that the blowback is falling on people, groups, communities and causes I genuinely care about. I recognize it’s far too late for me to mitigate all the damage I’ve done, but I’m determined to try to do what I can.
“I hid the truth or outright lied about my background to everyone in my life. There is not a single person on this planet … who knew what I was doing … The fact that I lied about who I was does not mean anyone else who speaks up for Palestine is lying and does not erase the urgency of listening to voices on the ground, voices who are courageously telling us about an ongoing genocide, even as the state of Israel deliberately targets journalists and others who are speaking the truth for extermination,” she continued.
The Guardian has reached out to Gann for additional comment.
Videos and local news articles online showed Gann’s involvement over the years in local pro-Palestinian activism, with one Facebook video posted by RJOC in November 2025 featuring Gann addressing attendees at a teach-in.
“Philly Educators for Palestine is bigger and stronger than ever before. Curious about who we are and what our purpose is? Listen to these powerful words from one of our founders, Hannah Gann, as she welcomed attendees to our most recent teach-in,” the video caption said.
Gann, who teaches at Philadelphia’s Workshop School, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer, was also the subject of a moving billboard outside her school in 2024. The mobile display featured a photo of her wearing a keffiyeh alongside the words: “Hannah Gann: 10th Grade Teacher & Philadelphia’s Leading Antisemite,” the grassroots outlet Rethinking Schools reported.
The Philadelphia Inquirer, which reviewed a document compiled by the Philly Palestine Coalition, noted that Gann often made references to alleged Palestinian relatives “including a Palestinian-born grandfather whom the PPC found was actually born in Baltimore, citing historical draft records and her great-grandfather’s US naturalization papers”.
Meanwhile, a former University of Pennsylvania classmate told the Philadelphia Inquirer that Gann was known in college “as a self-proclaimed white Jewish woman with family in the occupied West Bank. I watched her sudden transformation after she returned to Philly from the Peace Corps [in Rwanda]. She was clearly making herself look darker using makeup and fake tan, and speaking using [African American Vernacular English.]”
In a statement to the Guardian, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia school district said: “The school district of Philadelphia is aware of social media posts concerning a district employee and her involvement with an outside advocacy organization. The posts reference the employee’s involvement in an external group. The district is making support available to The Workshop School staff and students, as needed.”

Trump welcomes Xi to Washington as US, China agree to extend trade truce
Trump takes rare step of meeting foreign leader at the airport, underscoring the significance of US-China relationship.
China’s Xi visits US as Trump bets on stabilising global relations
United States President Donald Trump has welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to Washington, DC, for a three-day visit and high-stakes talks on trade, Taiwan and artificial intelligence.
Xi’s landed at Joint Base Andrews, outside the US capital, on Wednesday as the Trump administration announced that the two countries have agreed to extend an 11-month trade deal that offered temporary relief from punishing tariffs.

- list 2 of 3What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
- list 3 of 3As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
Trump took the rare step of personally meeting Xi on his arrival, marking the first time in 11 years that a US president has greeted a foreign leader at the base, according to US media.
At the arrival ceremony, the leaders and their wives shook hands, spoke for a few minutes and stood for pictures as a military band played, cannons blasted and a B-1 military bomber flew overhead.
In a written statement afterwards, Xi said China and the US should be partners and not rivals, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. “He said that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world,” Xinhua reported.
Trump’s in-person greeting signals the significance that Washington ascribes to its relationship with Beijing, whose meteoric economic rise over the last several decades has transformed it into a global superpower capable of rivalling the US.
Xi’s visit comes after he hosted Trump in Beijing in May.
His schedule in Washington, DC, will include a state dinner attended by leaders of the US’s powerful tech industry, a military ceremony at the White House and a visit to the National Archives, home to documents of historical and cultural significance such as the US Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.
His talks with Trump are likely to cover the US-Israel war on Iran, the US-China trade deal, AI, and US ties to Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, according to analysts.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday that he had met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of Xi’s visit to “see if we could do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series of smaller things”.
“We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement,” Bessent said.
The agreement, which was set to expire on November 10, has now been extended to January 10, he said.
Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, said the short extension suggests the two nations were planning a wider deal.
“The two sides indeed have a bigger scope of negotiation coming to their trade deals, and they need more time to negotiate the technicalities,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that the truce was expected to hold even before the trip began.
Sun called Xi’s visit to the US “unprecedented”, saying “there has never been any precedent in the history of US-China relations for the top two leaders of the two countries to visit each other within a single year”. She described the stabilisation of ties as “quite prominent and very impressive”, noting that only 12 months ago, the two countries were escalating tariffs and export controls against each other.
On Taiwan, Sun said Beijing’s main goal would be to prevent or stall a $14bn arms package that Congress approved earlier this year, but the Trump administration has been unwilling to advance.
She said she expected the most progress on AI, where the two governments could agree on ways to manage their dialogue.
“We know that the US has proposed a hotline mechanism for notification to each other when there is a significant security risk associated with AI that happens in their individual country,” she said. “We’ll have to see whether the two leaders are able to make progress on this important issue.”

Tigray forces launch offensive against Ethiopian government
Tigray People’s Liberation Front seizes control of airports and targets government positions in Afar and Amhara regions.
Tigrayan rebels have seized control of airports in the Tigray region in northern Ethiopia and launched an offensive against federal forces in the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions, according to officials.
Getachew Reda, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) has “launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara” early on Wednesday.

- list 3 of 3US lifts sanctions on Eritrea ‘to advance US regional interests’ in Red Sea
In a post on X, Getachew said the TPLF have “taken over federally controlled airports in Tigray leading to the suspension of flights to and from Tigray”.
“The TPLF politico-military leadership has obviously taken irresponsibility to new heights,” he added.
The Tigray regional government, however, said it was countering an “invasion” by federal forces.
In a statement posted on Facebook, it accused federal troops of “intensive bombardments” on Tuesday involving “aircraft, drones, and artillery”.
“The Tigray army has been instructed to counter the attack and genocidal invasion launched against us, and has entered into a defensive battle,” the statement added.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined after Abiy took office, triggering a devastating civil war from 2020 to 2022. The conflict killed about 600,000 people, according to estimates by the African Union, before the Pretoria Peace Agreement ended hostilities.
Clashes in Afar and Amhara
On Wednesday, clashes were under way in various parts of Afar, including the towns of Abala and Erebti, the AFP news agency reported, citing humanitarian workers in the region. In Amhara, federal forces were firing heavy weapons from a camp in the town of Lalibela, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two residents.
The offensive came after the TPLF announced on Sunday that it had allied with six other armed groups across Ethiopia to overthrow Abiy’s government.
Reuters, citing government and diplomatic sources, reported that Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside the Fano militia in Amhara.
Fano is a member of the new alliance with the TPLF.
It had sided with the federal government during the 2020-2022 war, but rose up against it in 2023 in an ongoing armed conflict that has resulted in thousands of deaths.
Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, told Reuters that members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while with the financial backing of Ethiopia’s neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea.
Eritrea has repeatedly denied similar accusations.
At the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Ethiopian President Taye Atske-Selassie Amde said his country had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours despite foreign interference.
“Our message to forces of destruction and mayhem is loud and clear. We urge them to respect the sacred right of the people of the Horn of Africa to live in peace and prosperity,” he said.
Analysts warned that the renewed hostilities could destabilise the region, which has still not recovered from the previous war. About one million people remain displaced in the region.
Alan Boswell, Horn of Africa director at the International Crisis Group, said allegations of Eritrea’s backing of the TPLF could trigger a regional conflict.
“Eritrea is also quite close, for instance, with the Sudanese army, and relations between Ethiopia and the Sudanese army have also been deteriorating,” Boswell said, adding that Ethiopia is also getting more involved in the civil war in Sudan, at least along its border.
“So this is all becoming one big regional mess, and it could get very, very ugly if we don’t see de-escalation.”

Sept. 23 (UPI) -- U.S. President Donald Trump greeted President Xi Jinping of China on Wednesday evening as the Chinese leader arrived at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, marking the start of a three-day state visit.
The tarmac greeting was a rare gesture for an incumbent U.S. president to a foreign leader. Trump and first lady Melania Trump met Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on a red carpet as the U.S. Air Force band performed the countries' national anthems. The ceremony also included a cannon salute, a 21-person honor cordon, color guards and a flyover by two B1 bombers.
There will be another ceremony Thursday morning at the White House featuring more than 500 U.S. service members. The presidents will meet Thursday afternoon with a state dinner Thursday night.
Both Republicans and Democrats have criticized the visit and the lavishness of Trump's treatment of the Chinese leader, The Hill reported . Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said onthe Senate floor Tuesday that Trump should remember that Xi "is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."
A statement by a group of Senate Democrats including Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., also criticized Trump's red-carpet treatment of the Chinese leader.
"President Xi gets the royal treatment while President Trump hurls threats and wages trade wars on allies like Canada," they wrote. "This is not leadership, and Americans deserve better."
The Democrats called on Trump to end China's access "to the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment it needs to build dangerous AI systems," stand with Taiwan against China and press Xi to stop supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.
The trip marks XI's first state visit to the United States in 11 years.

articles.title_orig: Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
articles.title_zh: Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
articles.content_orig:
Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.
Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
This year’s Meta Connect featured a new lightweight VR wearable and camera-free Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.
You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.
Meta’s latest wearable offers full virtual reality in a smart glasses-style form factor. Unlike a typical VR headset, the VR Glasses don’t have any straps, and Meta says they’re “five times lighter than Meta Quest 3” at just 100g. Similar to Google’s Project Aura, the glasses are tethered to a pocket-sized puck with the compute hardware, battery, and storage, including a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, 128GB of storage, and 12GB of RAM. The 5K micro OLED “Infinite Display” has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye, with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
The Meta VR Glasses are launching in spring 2027 for $1,299, pricier than the Meta Ray-Ban Display but less expensive than the Apple Vision Pro, while offering similar features. Users can connect the glasses to a Mac or Windows laptop for use as a virtual external display, with an option for a virtual surface keyboard and touchpad.
The VR Glasses also have access to the full Meta Quest catalog of apps and games and support for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meta says the glasses are “the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever,” and users will be able to watch “immersive live sports” with them as well as 3D movies. They even have a “hologram” feature that creates a “photorealistic digital version of your face” for using in calls while wearing the glasses, reminiscent of the “personas” on the Apple Vision Pro.
Meta is launching camera-free smart glasses
The highlight of the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the feature they don’t have: built-in cameras. You can use them for things like listening to music, taking calls, or chatting with an AI assistant, but they can’t take pictures or record video — features that have sparked privacy and harassment concerns around Meta’s other glasses.
Meta says the new audio-only glasses are also its “lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet,” weighing just 43g. They offer up to 12 hours of battery life per charge, or 48 hours with the charging case. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio will launch on October 13th starting at $349 with 23 different color and lens combinations.
Refreshed Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 arrive with battery and design upgrades
Meta launched an updated version of its main Ray-Ban Meta glasses, starting at $449. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offer up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than the Gen 2. They also have “a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI” and a new six-mic array that Meta says “cuts more than 90% of background noise.”
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 has a slimmer design than the Gen 2 as well, with 27 color and lens combinations, including new Zena and Aviator frame styles. Notably, one thing that hasn’t changed is the built-in LED light that indicates when the glasses are recording, which Meta rolled out a privacy fix for last month.
Budget glasses launch along with new glasses styles
Alongside its pricier Ray-Ban glasses, Meta also announced some updates to its in-house line of glasses. It’s launching a new lower-cost version of the Meta Adventurer, which will start at $249 for a basic design with black frames and gray lenses, launching October 23rd.
Meta is also introducing a new “Mix & Match” program for customizing its glasses with different frames, lenses, and case colors. Plus, its EssilorLuxottica collection is getting two new styles, Capri and Nova, and the Kylie Jenner Starfire frames are getting a new ivory colorway. Meta’s also launching a new collaboration collection with Lisa of Blackpink.
Meta Glasses are expanding to more countries starting today, too, including Singapore, South Korea, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates, with availability in Brazil “coming soon.”
Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to more regions with some new features
A year after they originally launched, the Meta Ray-Ban Display are coming to more regions. The glasses are on sale in the UK and Canada starting today, and they’ll be available in France, Italy, and Germany starting on October 13th. Meta’s also introducing online ordering for customers in those regions and the US.
Meta’s launching a new Explore app for Display glasses where users will be able to “browse and use a growing selection of experiences built for your glasses.” The Meta Ray-Ban Display is also getting photo editing, an improved calendar, and mirrored phone notifications. Plus, Meta says the “hologram” feature launching on its VR Glasses is rolling out on the Meta Ray-Ban Display “in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”
After launching its new Muse assistant earlier this month, Meta says it’s “working on” bringing the AI to its smart glasses. When it arrives on the glasses, Muse will be able to do things like guide your workouts, log meals, book appointments, and “help buy products you see.”
Meta also announced some new features for Muse, including video calls with a customizable live avatar of the AI. Plus, Muse agents are getting their own email addresses for completing tasks and communicating with users.
Meta is making an AI ‘charm’
Mark Zuckerberg teased one last device, Muse Charm, a small AI gadget that houses the Muse agent and looks a little bit like a supersized Tamagotchi. More details will be shared “soon,” he said, but the product is supposed to ship in time for the holiday season.

articles.title_orig: Idaho case may be connected to the 1982 Tylenol murders, officials say
articles.title_zh: Idaho case may be connected to the 1982 Tylenol murders, officials say
articles.content_orig:
An unknown man walked into the Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Boise on Dec. 4, 1982.
He wore a Seiko watch, a leather belt and a bolo tie made of turquoise and silver. He carried a wallet but no identification. An envelope filled with 19 $100 bills sat inside his shirt pocket. His hair was dyed and he had a deep tan, not common in the Idaho winter.
Within hours, he died by suicide inside the church. The cause was cyanide poisoning.
The Ada County sheriff’s office has spent decades searching for the man’s identity. At a Wednesday morning news conference, they announced they’ve uncovered the identity of the “Unknown Wanderer” and that he may be connected to the 1982 Tylenol murders. Illinois investigators, however, remain highly skeptical, pointing to a lack of physical evidence.
“The reliance on psychological profiles to prove a crime is no more reliable than the reliance of tarot cards or seeing how chicken bones line up in the dirt,” said former federal prosecutor Jeremy Margolis, who was a key player in the original task force in 1982.
Seven Chicago-area residents died after swallowing Tylenol capsules laced with potassium cyanide in September 1982. Widely regarded as an act of domestic terrorism — a term not in the country’s vernacular at the time — the murders led to tamper-evident packaging, copycat killings and myths about tainted Halloween candy. No one has been charged with the murders. The lone suspect died in 2023.
Tim Cooper, a detective with the Ada County sheriff’s office, said he reopened the “Unknown Wanderer” case in 2019 after a member of the Sacred Heart church approached him. He combed through 17,000 missing person records but it was an engraved key located with the man’s belongings that finally helped crack the case, he said.
He connected the key to Jacksonville, Florida, using its markings and etchings. There, detectives found a property owner who had gone missing in 1982 and was declared deceased in absentia seven years later.
They compared DNA from the missing man’s brother with the man who died in the Boise church. It found that the two men had the same father, Cooper said.
Cooper said they were then able to determine the “Unknown Wanderer” was Dr. Mathew Francis Betkouski.
Betkouski, an organic chemist, was by all accounts a “brilliant man” and had a documented fascination with explosives, Cooper alleged. Betkouski came from a prominent Los Angeles family.
In 1974, Betkouski sustained a traumatic brain injury that worsened his mental health problems, Cooper said. Co-workers at Flavors & Fragrances in the Jacksonville area reported him for discussing the “perfect crime” and that “cyanide could be used as a less messy means of taking one’s life,” Cooper alleged. He was later fired from the job.
“Dr. Betkouski was observed talking to himself on occasions and had fears that he was being tracked,” Cooper said.
Betkouski was terminated from another job in New Mexico in 1982, Cooper said. A fellow scientist recalled a comment from Betkouski that poison could be introduced into over-the-counter capsules. Betkouski also is believed to have taken home unauthorized material from the lab, Cooper alleged.
In recent years, detectives were able to examine Betkouski’s remaining items that his brother kept at his home in Los Angeles. In his desk, they found photos, letters, a map of Chicago and a small bottle of cyanide with a handwritten label.
Although heavily implied, officers at the news conference stopped short of labeling Betkouski as a suspect in the Tylenol murders. For one, Cooper said the cyanide they found in his desk was sodium cyanide, not potassium cyanide, which was the type used in the poisonings.
They also couldn’t prove Betkouski visited the Chicago area in 1982. The most recent pictures they found of him in the area are believed to be from December 1981, Cooper said. He also mentioned that Betkouski supposedly talked to a priest at the Boise church, but that the priest never gave an official statement to investigators.
“We have heard various things that may have been said or done in the church that day, and some are interesting,” Cooper said. “But in the end, we cannot independently verify what was or wasn’t said in the confessional on the day Dr. Betkouski died.”
The sheriff’s department also brought up forensic psychiatrist Dr. Park Dietz, who shared his belief that Betkouski committed the Tylenol murders. He said Betkouski’s brain injury made him more paranoid. Betkouski also allegedly indicated in a letter that “scenes of violence could produce euphoria,” which demonstrates a possible motive for such a violent event, Dietz theorized.
He said he presented the evidence to other forensic psychiatrists and criminal profilers who also labeled Betkouski as a “viable suspect.”
“It’s an extraordinary thing to have been around at the beginning in 1982, and now today in 2026 to see very likely closure,” Dietz said.
However, the news conference did not persuade current and former investigators with deep ties to the case, as Idaho law enforcement did not offer any physical evidence connecting Betkouski to the killings. They also downplayed the psychological profile outlined by Dietz.
“It was clear from the press conference that Idaho law enforcement, which does not regard the man as a suspect in the Tylenol murders, found no credible evidence he was involved in the Tylenol murders,” said Margolis, the former federal prosecutor.
Multiple law enforcement sources told the Tribune that Illinois authorities had compared Betkouski’s DNA with profiles found on the poisoned Tylenol bottles in recent years, but there was no match. The police task force formed in the wake of the 1982 killings also looked at the Idaho case at the time of Betkouski’s suicide but did not find any connection.
When asked at the news conference if the department was collaborating with the Arlington Heights Police Department, which has been the lead agency on the case, Ada County Sheriff Matt Clifford said they communicated with them early on but that they haven’t heard from them “in quite some time now and I couldn’t tell you why.”
He said the department also shared its findings with Chicago police.
“It’s not our job to name him as a suspect. This is not an Idaho case. The Tylenol killers case remains with Chicago because that’s their job,” Clifford said. “We’ve sent everything to them and what they do with it is whatever they want to do. If they use it and rule him out then we’re all OK with that too.”
He said instead that additional details of the possible connection would be released in an Unsolved Mysteries documentary called “Unmasking the Tylenol Killer” that releases Oct. 9 on Roku.
“So I’m not going to beat around the bush with everybody, but this isn’t over, and what you’ve heard today could take months or even years to fully work through,” Clifford said.
Christopher Sefton, acting deputy chief of the Arlington Heights Police Department, said they received and reviewed Ada County’s information and that they “remain committed to collaborating with our law enforcement partners and pursuing any viable leads as they become available.” A Chicago police spokesperson also confirmed they’d been in contact with them.
An FBI spokesperson shared a stronger stance. The spokesperson said there have been “repeated claims over the past 44 years about alleged links to the Tylenol Murders which have (remained) unsubstantiated.”
“Out of respect for the ongoing, legitimate investigation, those impacted by the tragedy, and the law enforcement partners who have provided genuine support since the start, the FBI remains the lead on investigating and releasing credible information to the public once the evidence yields a true case resolution,” the spokesperson said.
Illinois authorities have instead long identified James Lewis as the lone suspect in the Tylenol investigation.
As the Tribune first reported, Lewis’ body was found in his downtown Cambridge condominium in July 20

articles.title_orig: Meta is trying VR glasses (again), this time with more IMAX
articles.title_zh: Meta is trying VR glasses (again), this time with more IMAX
articles.content_orig:
Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing. At its Connect event on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market, which will be available next spring starting at $1,299.99.
These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility.
Moments before unveiling them, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile ago to shift its focus away from the Metaverse and build fewer VR devices until it had real breakthroughs.
“This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.”
Meta says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal eyewear than the bulky headsets the company has released before. The frames are made of magnesium alloy, and the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They connect to a computing puck that doubles as a battery, which users can just slip the puck into their pocket to use the glasses on the go.
The glasses are largely built for entertainment. Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support. Users will be able to download and watch movies.
Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films.
Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX-enhanced certified VR device ever” and says they will be one of the few ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines IMAX’s distinct high-resolution viewing experience.
The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user’s physical space into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D.
Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience.
The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you’ll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures.
